newsitem.title: CHINA: China defends soaring foreign exchange reserves.
newsitem.headline: China defends soaring foreign exchange reserves.

text.p: China's top foreign exchange official defended on Monday the central policy of purchasing surplus hard currency to stabilise the exchange rate while expanding foreign exchange reserves.

"It may not be the only correct policy combination to actively attract foreign capital, stabilise the exchange rate and increase hard currency reserves," the Xinhua news agency quoted Zhou Xiaochuan, director of the State Administration of Foreign Exchange (SAFE), as saying.
"But right now it's the correct policy for China, in view of a sustained and robust capital influx," Zhou told a meeting of local foreign exchange administration officials in Beijing.

The People's Bank of China, the central bank, has bought surplus foreign exchange on the market to prevent the yuan from appreciating too much since China ended a two-tier exchange system and devalued the yuan in 1994.
China's foreign exchange reserves have soared to $105 billion at the end of 1996, the largest in the world after Japan, from $21.2 billion at the end of 1993 and $73.56 billion at the end of 1995.
Zhou acknowledged the costs of maintaining such large reserves, but said the size had boosted China's international payments ability.
Central bank governor Dai Xianglong has also defended the size of the reserves.
Despite the $30 billion increase in the reserves last year, the central bank's discount loans to the four big state-owned commercial banks dropped by 60 billion yuan, he was quoted as saying.
"Overall, the term structure of China's foreign exchange reserves was reasonable and the return on the hard currencies was fairly good," Dai was quoted as saying.
